newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Denktash calls new Cyprus talks "soundings" only.
newsitem.headline: Denktash calls new Cyprus talks "soundings" only.

text.p: Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash said he regarded Wednesday's talks with Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides only as "soundings" and that major issues should be left to subsequent rounds.

Denktash, in a late Monday interview with Reuters, also made clear he holds fast to his demand for recognition of his community's sovereign equality with the Greek Cypriots, whose administration is internationally recognised as the legitimate government of the entire island.
Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since troops from Turkey took over the north of the island in 1974 in reaction to a coup in Nicosia backed by the junta then ruling Greece.

Denktash, who refuses to recognise Clerides's government as speaking for the whole of Cyprus, is president of a Turkish Cypriot state proclaimed in 1983 but recognised only by Turkey. The United Nations has been trying for decades to reunite the island as a bi-communal, bi-zonal federation.
Referring to U.N.-sponsored talks due to take place from July 9 to 13 at a rural resort called Troutbeck, 90 miles (145 kms) north of New York city, Denktash said:

"If we keep this round as a round for sounding and not attempt to tackle the issues which are obviously difficult ones for both sides, and if sounding results in some sort of mutual understanding on some of the issues, then I think we shall have a chance of going to the second round."
"Hopefully, if at this round we don't break down, we shall have a second round, we are told, in Geneva, in August."
Noting he and Clerides last meet nearly three years ago in Nicosia, he added, "I couldn't go half a mile to meet Mr Clerides. And I had to come 3,000 miles for all this nonsense."
"But I am glad I did because I got my digital camera," joked Denktash, an avid photographer who delighted in demonstrating his latest acquisition.
The 73-year-old Denktash and Clerides, 78, have known -- and battled each other -- for nearly half a century, since both were young London-trained barristers.

Asked whether his demand for recognition of Turkish Cypriot sovereignty must be on the negotiating table, Denktash replied: "It has always been on the table. We are asking the Greek Cypriot side to recognise that, since the two sides are expected to establish a federation by giving up certain of their rights to a central government jointly."

Alluding to the breakdown in 1963 of a government that included representatives of both communities, he said: "We have been ruling ourselves for 34 years, even before we established our state.How can they say we are not sovereign ?.They have to have to accept it, as we are accepting them as a sovereign Greek Cypriot community, if they want to establish a sovereign federation."
Denktash took issue with talks, set for next year, on the Nicosia's government's request to join the European Union.

"We hope and expect European Union countries to have a second look at the Cyprus problem and to decide whether Cyprus as a whole has applied or not," he said. "Then they will see that Cyprus has not applied, Greek Cypriots have applied."

He said if talks on EU membership got under way "we shall start immediate negotiations with Turkey for the same kind of union with Turkey. And we shall stop all contacts with Greek Cypriots because that means there is no hope of a settlement."
Denktash questioned the timing of the Cyprus talks saying it was "impossible to expect a solution very soon when Mr. Clerides is waiting for his elections" next February.

He speculated that one reason for holding the talks now was "because everybody has realised that Cyprus is heading into a direct area of conflict by the time the EU negotiations start and the missiles arrive" -- a reference to Russian-made S-300 air defence missiles that the Nicosia government expects to deploy next year. Turkey has vowed to prevent this.

Denktash, who spent about an hour Monday with Richard Holbrooke, the U.S. presidential emissary for Cyprus and an architect of the 1995 Bosnia peace accords, described their meeting as "very friendly" and "a sincere exchange of views."
Asked whether it had also been a meeting of minds, he replied: "I think a meeting of friends rather than minds."
